extracted.intended_audience: authors, editors, compositors, typesetters, and publishers preparing manuscripts, indexes, tables, and proofs for publication
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and detailed practical rules for preparing and composing books and journal matter: footnotes, indexing, tabular work, spacing, type/style usage, indentation, proofs, make-up, and typesetting-machine practice. Intended to guide authors, editors, and compositors in preparing copy and proofs for press.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of consonant combinations (syllabification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Other combinations of consonants are divided (examples given: Trpd<r-cr(D, eA-Trts, ev-Bov, dp-jxa-Ta).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When dividing words for syllabification, separate other combinations of consonants between syllables as shown by the examples. Apply consistent division to similar consonant clusters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compound words divided into original parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Compound words are divided into their original parts; subject to that the foregoing rule applies (examples: Trpoa-d-yu), nap-d-yw).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When hyphenating or dividing compound words, separate at the component boundaries first, then apply the general syllabification/division rules within each component.

rubrics_metrics.name: Latin: count vowels and diphthongs as syllables
rubrics_metrics.description: A Latin word has as many syllables as it has vowels or diphthongs {ae, au, oe, ei, eu, ui).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When syllabifying Latin words, treat each vowel or diphthong as a separate syllable unit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Latin: divide before single consonant between vowels
rubrics_metrics.description: When a single consonant occurs between two vowels, divide before the consonant (examples: Cae-sar, me-ri-di-es).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For Latin words with V-C-V sequences, place the break before the consonant (V | C V).

rubrics_metrics.name: Latin: divide before last consonant in clusters (with exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the case of two or more consonants divide before the last consonant, except in the combinations: mute (p, ph, b, t, th, d, c, ch, g) + liquid (l, r), and qu or gu (examples: om-nis, scrip-tus, cun-c-tus, but: pa-tris, e-quus, lin-gua).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For consonant clusters in Latin, split before the final consonant except when the cluster is a mute+liquid or qu/gu, which remain together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Latin compounds: separate into elements then apply rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Compound words are separated first into their component elements, and within each element the foregoing rules apply (examples: ad-est, ab-rum-po, red-e-o, trans-i-go).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat Latin compounds by first splitting into roots/prefixes/suffixes, then syllabify each element according to the above Latin rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of superior figures for reference indexes
rubrics_metrics.description: For reference indexes, as a rule, use superior figures. Only in special cases should asterisks, daggers, etc., be employed; for instance, in tabular or algebraic matter, where figures would be likely to cause confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer superscript (superior) numerals for footnote/index markers in running text; reserve symbols (asterisk, dagger) for special situations where numerals would interfere with comprehension (e.g., tables, algebraic matter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of index figures in text
rubrics_metrics.description: Index figures in the text should be placed after the punctuation marks, without space, except in German, where they are placed inside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Put the superscript reference number immediately after the punctuation ending the cited phrase or sentence (no intervening space), except follow German convention for placement inside punctuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequence of non-figure index symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: When figures are not used, the sequence of indexes should be: * (asterisk or "star"), † (dagger), ‡ (double dagger), § (section mark), || (parallels), ¶ (paragraph mark).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If using symbol markers instead of figures, follow this specified order to avoid ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ibid. / loc. cit. / op. cit.
rubrics_metrics.description: Where references to the same work follow each other closely and uninterruptedly, use ihid. (ibid.) instead of repeating the title. Ihid. takes the place of as much of the previous reference as is repeated. Ihid. should, however, not ordinarily be used for the first footnote on a verso (left-hand) page; it is better usage either to repeat the title, if short, or to use loc. cit. (when reference is to entire citation) or op. cit. (when work only is cited).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'ibid.' for immediate, consecutive citations to the same source, but avoid 'ibid.' in certain positions (e.g., first footnote on a verso); prefer repeating short titles or using loc. cit./op. cit. where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Footnote placement and sizing for tables
rubrics_metrics.description: Footnotes to tables, whether the tables are ruled or open, should be in 6-pt., and should invariably be placed at the foot of the table and not at the foot of the page. For reference indexes in such cases use asterisks, etc., and not superior figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table footnotes must be small (6-pt) and located immediately under the table; use symbol markers (asterisk, dagger) for table-specific notes rather than superscript numerals which may conflict with running text footnote numbering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not repeat author's name in footnote if in text
rubrics_metrics.description: If the author's name is given in the text in connection with a reference to, or a quotation from, his work, it should not be repeated in the footnote.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omit the author's name in the footnote when the name already appears in the running text adjacent to the citation or quotation to avoid redundancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place index figure at end of quotation
rubrics_metrics.description: It is better to place the index figure in the text at the end of the quotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place the footnote marker after the closing quotation mark or at the end of the quoted passage rather than mid-quotation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviations and numeral systems in references
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinarily, omit 'Vol.,' 'chap.,' and 'p.' in references to particular passages. Use Roman numerals (capitals) for Volume, Book, Part, and Division, except in reference to ancient, classical authors or works, when lower-case roman numerals should be used; Roman numerals (lower-case) for chapter and pages of introductory matter (Preface, etc.); and Arabic numerals for number (Heft) and text pages. Only when confusion would be liable to arise, or in exceptional cases, use 'Vol.,' 'p.,' etc.; but where the reference is to a page unaccompanied by further details, the abbreviation 'p.' or 'pp.' must of course be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the specified conventions for when to include abbreviations and which numeral forms to use for different kinds of divisions (volumes, chapters, preface pages, etc.), and deviate only to avoid ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classical references punctuation conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: In classical references use no comma between author's name and the title of his work; and no comma following the title, unless 'Vol.,' 'p.,' or some kindred symbol is used. In all references to divisions of classical or ancient works, use periods in place of commas, reserving the comma to indicate a succession (of pages, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When citing classical/ancient works adhere to the compact punctuation style: omit commas between author and title; use periods between divisions (I.II.III) rather than commas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Date placement in periodical references
rubrics_metrics.description: The date of publication in a reference to a periodical should immediately follow the volume number, and should be put in parentheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Format periodical citations so that volume number is followed immediately by the year in parentheses: e.g., Journal Name, 30 (1902).

rubrics_metrics.name: Footnote numbering conventions for linotype composition
rubrics_metrics.description: In work set on the linotype machine footnotes should be numbered consecutively through an article, in a journal, or through a chapter, in a book, to save resetting in case of change. Note exceptions: Botanical Gazette and Astrophysical Journal use other styles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Number footnotes consecutively for the practical benefit of typesetting, except where a journal specifies an alternative convention; check journal-specific rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing: treatment of M', Mc, Mac, St., Ste.
rubrics_metrics.description: Names beginning with M', Mc, Mac, or St., Ste., whether the following letter is capitalized or not, should be listed as if the prefix were spelled Mac, Saint, Sainte.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In alphabetical indexes normalize such prefixes so users need not search multiple places — treat M', Mc, Mac as Mac; St./Ste. as Saint/Sainte.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing: compound names listed under first part
rubrics_metrics.description: Compound names should be listed under the first part of the name. List the other parts of the names in their respective alphabetical positions and give a cross-reference to the first (examples: Campbell-Bannerman, Sir Henry; Lloyd-George, David and cross-ref 'George, Lloyd-, David. Sec Lloyd-George').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Index compound (hyphenated) surnames under the first element and provide cross-references from other alphabetic positions to the primary entry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing: hyphenated names adopted gratuitously
rubrics_metrics.description: In the case of hyphenated names gratuitously adopted, as in the case of married women adding the maiden name to the married name, the name preceding the hyphen may be disregarded, and listing should be under the letter of the true name, with a cross-reference under the name preceding the hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a hyphenated name is adopted (not intrinsic to the original name), index under the person's true name and provide a cross-reference under the hyphenated form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing: prefixes rule with exceptions by language
rubrics_metrics.description: Names with prefixes should be listed under the part following the prefix, except (i) in English (see above); (ii) in French when the prefix consists of or contains the article; (iii) in Italian and Spanish when the prefix consists simply of the article; (iv) in Dutch, the 'Van,' 'Ten,' etc., being always capitalized; (v) when the prefix and the name are written as one word. Naturalized names with prefixes should be treated according to the rules for the language adopted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Index prefixes as part of the following element except in enumerated linguistic exceptions; adhere to language-specific conventions and treat naturalized names according to the adopted language's rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing: umlauted letters treated as digraphs
rubrics_metrics.description: Names spelled with the umlaut ä, ö, ü should be listed as if the umlaut were spelled out ae, oe, ue (examples: Müller as Mueller).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat Germanic umlauted names in indices as though the vowel were doubled with an 'e' to ensure consistent alphabetization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing: names connected by 'and' or equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: Names having two parts, or names of firms, connected by 'and', '&', 'y' (Spanish), 'et' (French), 'und' (German), or 'e' (Italian), should be listed according to the first letter of the name preceding the connective (examples: Smith & Evans under 'S'; Gomez y Pineda under 'G').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For compound firm names, index them by the first principal name (the element before the connective) to maintain findability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tables: choice of point size for open and ruled tables
rubrics_metrics.description: In 12-pt. and 10-pt. matter open (unruled) tables should ordinarily be set in 9-pt, leaded; ruled, in 8-pt, solid. In 9-pt matter both open and ruled tables should be set in 8-pt. solid. In 8-pt matter open tables should be set in 6-pt. leaded; ruled, in 6-pt. solid. In 6-pt. matter both open and ruled tables should be set in 6-pt. solid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select table type sizes to harmonize with body text: use slightly smaller type for table bodies, with open tables commonly a point larger and leaded when readability requires it; use 6-8-9-pt mappings as practical guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Table captions and box-heads sizing and style
rubrics_metrics.description: Captions for the columns of open tables and box-heads for ruled tables should ordinarily be set in 6-pt. Box-heads of open tables should be 6-pt. caps and lower case unless subheads are used, in which case caps and small caps are used for the upper head; in ruled tables with box-heads of several stories, the upper story — primary heads — should be set in caps and small caps, except where the second story consists of figures only; the lower — secondary — in caps and lower case. Wherever small caps are used in box-heads, the heading for the 'stub' (i.e., first column) should, as a rule, also be set in caps and small caps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use small, consistent typography for table heads (commonly 6-pt), applying caps/small-caps hierarchy for multi-story heads and matching stub headings to the style used in box-heads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spacing between rules and table matter
rubrics_metrics.description: In ruled tables there should be at least two leads' space between the horizontal rules and the matter inclosed, and, if practicable, at least the equivalent of an en quad, of the type in which the body of the table is set, between the perpendicular rules and the matter inclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide generous clearance between table rules (lines) and the enclosed text: minimum two leads vertically and about an en quad horizontally to avoid cramped appearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of periods or leaders between columns in open tables
rubrics_metrics.description: In open tables either periods, one em apart and aligned, or leaders, may be used between the columns. In ruled tables, in the 'stub,' leaders should usually be employed, if there is room, except in case the stub runs over and a brace is necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For open tables consider aligned periods or typographic leaders to guide the eye across columns; in ruled tables employ leaders in the stub for clarity unless structural considerations prevent it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment of figures and representation of blanks
rubrics_metrics.description: In ruled columns of figures, to express a blank use leaders across the full width of the column. Center the figures in the column; if they cannot be put in the exact center, and there is an unequal number of digits in the groups, leave more space on the left than on the right. All decimals and dollar signs or other concrete values should be aligned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Align numeric data carefully: center (or align by decimals), use leaders to indicate intentional blanks, and ensure decimal points and currency symbols line up vertically for easy comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading-matter in table columns: centering and run-over handling
rubrics_metrics.description: When there is reading-matter in the columns of a ruled table, it should be centered, if possible; if any line runs over, use hanging indention, and align all on the left.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Center short running text in table cells for neatness; when lines wrap, apply hanging indents and left-align wrapped lines for readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of double vs single rules in tables
rubrics_metrics.description: Double rules should be used at the top of all tables, but perpendicularly, as a usual thing, only when a table is doubled up on itself and the stub is repeated. In continued broadside tables where the heading is not repeated use a single rule only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply double rules at top of tables for emphasis; avoid vertical double rules except in repeated-stub situations; use single rules for continued broadside tables.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to set tables open vs ruled and continuation rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Tables of two columns only should be set open; of three or more, ruled, except in such a case as the table on p. 99. All continuations of tables should be of the same dimensions, even if blank columns are necessary, and tables with identical headings should stand parallel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer open format for simple two-column tables and ruled format for more complex multi-column tables; ensure continuations match dimensions and align parallel with identical headings for consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Table numbering and headlines style
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Table I,' etc., in headlines of tables should ordinarily be set in caps of the type in which the body of the table is set and should not exceed the width of the table; the following (descriptive) line, if any, should be set in caps and small caps of the same type. A single descriptive headline, not preceded by the number of the table, should be set in caps of the type in which the table is set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Format table numbers and headlines compactly in caps and small caps; keep the table number within the table width and use consistent typographic hierarchy for descriptive lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Table footnotes formatting and repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: A footnote to the table should be set in 6-pt. with a paragraph indention, and should not exceed the width of the table. But when 6-pt. and 8-pt. ruled tables are both used in the same work, use 8-pt. headings over all tables. When tables containing footnotes run over several pages it is necessary to repeat the footnotes on each even page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep table footnotes small (6-pt) and within table width; if multiple table sizes are used adopt a uniform heading size; when a table continues across pages, repeat its footnotes on each even page to aid readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point system and pica standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The point is the underlying unit of all typographical measures. The standard of measurement is the pica. A pica is twelve points (one-sixth of an inch). Common names for sizes: 12-pt (pica), 11-pt (small pica), 10-pt (long primer), 9-pt (bourgeois), 8-pt (brevier), 7-pt (minion), 6-pt (nonpareil), 5-pt (agate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the point and pica system as the basis for specifying and comparing type sizes; refer to conventional size names when instructing compositors or describing type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Styles of type: roman, italic, boldface and manuscript indications
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinary type is called roman. Type with a sloping face is called italic or italics. Type with a heavy black face is called bold face. Italic is indicated in manuscripts by a straight line under the word or words; bold face is indicated by a wavy line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify type styles clearly in manuscripts using the given manuscript marking conventions (straight underline for italics, wavy line for bold) and use roman/italic/bold purposefully for emphasis and hierarchy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Font composition: caps, small caps, lower-case
rubrics_metrics.description: A font includes large capitals ('caps'), small capitals ('small caps'), and lower-case letters. Caps are indicated by three straight lines; small caps by two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When requesting small caps or caps ensure the compositor understands the font must include corresponding variants; use the indicated manuscript marks to specify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions of em, en, and other spaces
rubrics_metrics.description: An em (em quad) is a block the top of which forms a perfect square equal to type size; an en quad is half an em; a three-em space is one-third of an em and is the standard space used to separate words; a jour-em is one-fourth of an em; a five-em is one-fifth; a hair-space is any space thinner than a 5-em.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these standard definitions when specifying spacing requirements; apply the three-em (one-third em) space as the default interword space in foundry-type composition unless otherwise required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard intra-line spacing rules
rubrics_metrics.description: A standard line should have a 3-em space between all words not separated by other punctuation points than commas, and after commas; an en quad after semicolons, and colons followed by a lower-case letter; two 3-em spaces after colons followed by a capital; an em quad after periods, and exclamation and interrogation points, concluding a sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the specified spacing scheme to produce well-proportioned lines: majority 3-em interword spacing; larger quads after stronger punctuation to visually separate sentence elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjusting spacing: order of adjustments
rubrics_metrics.description: If necessary to reduce spacing in a line, begin with commas, and letters of slanting form — i.e., with a large 'shoulder' on the side adjoining the space; if necessary to increase, begin with overlapping letters — i.e., with 'kerns' protruding on the side adjoining the space — straight-up-and-down letters, and points other than periods and commas (in this order).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When tightening or loosening justification, adjust spaces adjacent to commas and slanted letters first when reducing, and expand near kerned (protruding) letters and punctuation when increasing, to preserve even optical color.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain proportion of good spacing; avoid alternating extremes
rubrics_metrics.description: In a well-spaced line, with a 3-em space between a majority of the words, there should not be more than an en quad between the rest; this proportion should be maintained in increasing or reducing. Do not follow an exceptionally thin-spaced line with an exceptionally wide-spaced one, or vice versa, if at all avoidable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for consistent spacing proportion across lines; avoid sudden changes in spacing from line to line which can be visually jarring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on hair-spacing or em-quad stretching to avoid run-over
rubrics_metrics.description: Never hair-space, or em-quad, a line to avoid a run-over.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not artificially compress lines using hair-spaces or em-quads solely to prevent an overflow; prefer reflowing, hyphenation, or editorial adjustment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not space out last line of paragraph
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not space out the last line of a paragraph allowing of an indention of an em or more at the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid stretching the last line of a paragraph to create excessive trailing space; use normal justification or reflow text instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short words spacing equality
rubrics_metrics.description: Short words, like 'a,' 'an,' etc., should have the same space on each side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure small words have uniform surrounding spaces to maintain consistent word color and rhythm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thin space usage with symbols and metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a thin space after §, *, [, and similar signs; before 'f.,' 'ff.,' and the metric symbols (examples: '§ 14. Be it further ordained . . .'; 'pp. 10 ff.; 16 cm.').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply thin spaces in compact notational contexts to improve legibility and avoid crowding adjacent symbols and abbreviations.

rubrics_metrics.name: No space between currency symbol and numerals in English/American sums
rubrics_metrics.description: In American and English sums of money no space is used between the symbols, $ and £ (pounds), s. (shillings), and d. (pence), and the numerals (an en leader is used for a decimal point): $2.75; £10 3.s. 2d.; 10° C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Format monetary amounts without space between symbol and number; align decimals with an en leader for decimal points where specified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spacing after numerals in headings and small-cap rules
rubrics_metrics.description: After Arabic and Roman numerals at the beginning of lines, denoting subsections, there should be an en quad. After Arabic and Roman numerals at the beginning of center-heads there should be an em quad. Small-cap headings should have an en quad between the words; cap-and-small-cap and cap-headings, two 3-em spaces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow these spacing norms for numerals and heading styles to maintain consistent hierarchy and alignment in headings and subsection markers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scripture reference spacing
rubrics_metrics.description: Scripture references should be spaced thus (use 9-unit colon): II Cor. 1:16-20; 2:5—3:12.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Format biblical citations with the specified spacing around colons (a 9-unit colon) to ensure clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: No space between letters forming products and superscripts/subscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Between letters forming products, and before superior figures or letters indicating powers, and inferior figures or letters, ordinarily no space should be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In mathematical/chemical notation keep multiplicative letters and power indicators tightly set without spaces for correct semantic reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indentation standards by measure and type size
rubrics_metrics.description: In linotype composition in measures of less than 10 picas' width, indent all sizes 1 em. In measures of from 10 to 20, ii-pt., 1 em; 10-pt., 1¼; 9-pt., 1⅛; 8-pt., 1⅛; 6-pt., 2. In measures of from 20 to 30, ii-pt., 1½ ems; 10-pt., 1½; 9-pt., 1⅝; 8-pt., 2; 6-pt., 2¼. This is for plain paragraphs. In monotype composition indentions should be such that all paragraph indentions align irrespective of the size of the type. Standard indents for measures of 19 to 30 picas are given (detailed mappings). Narrower measures proportionately less; wider proportionately more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the provided indentation table as practical standards for paragraph indents depending on measure width and point size; ensure monotype indent alignment across sizes and scale indent proportionally with measure width.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hanging indention standards and use
rubrics_metrics.description: In hanging indentions, in measures of less than 10 picas, indent all sizes 1 em; from 10 to 20, ii-pt., lo-pt., 9-pt., and 8-pt., 1½ ems; 6-pt., 2 ems; from 20 to 30, ii-pt., lo-pt., 9-pt., and 8-pt., 2 ems; 6-pt., 3 ems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use hanging indents with the stated dimensions based on measure width and type size when formatting bibliographies, lists, or paragraphs requiring a hanging format.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry indentation and alignment rules
rubrics_metrics.description: In poetry, center the longest line and let the indention be governed by that; where consecutive quotations vary slightly in length, indent all alike. Indent according to rhymes and length of lines. In blank verse, where the lines are approximately of the same length, they should be aligned. If consecutive lines rhyme, they should likewise be aligned; if rhymes alternate, indent rhyming lines alike; indent disproportionately short lines more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose poetry by visually centering on the longest line, align blank verse, align rhyming lines, and use indentation to reflect rhyme structure and line-length variations for balanced appearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for plain paragraphs; use of hanging for emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: In ordinary reading-matter 'plain paragraphs' are always preferable. Where it is desired to bring into relief the opening word or words of a paragraph, or the number introducing such paragraph, or where a center-head makes more than three lines, 'hanging indention' is often employed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Default to plain (first-line indented) paragraphs for readability; use hanging indention sparingly to emphasize opening words or for typographic necessity when headings occupy multiple lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead (leading) and slug definitions and standard sizes
rubrics_metrics.description: A lead is a strip of metal used to separate lines of type. The ordinary (standard) lead is 2 points thick. A slug is a strip of metal, thicker than a lead, used in the make-up of printed matter into pages, to be inserted after headlines, etc. The two standard sizes are 6 and 12 points thick.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use standard lead (2-pt) for typical line separation; use slugs for larger vertical spacing needs (6-pt and 12-pt) such as before/after headlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headings: center-head, side-head, cut-in head, box-head, running-head conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Center-heads are headlines placed at equal distances from both margins, usually set in caps or small caps and not followed by a period. When such center-head makes more than one line, either the (inverted) 'pyramid' form (for two or three lines) or 'hanging indention' (for more than three lines) is employed. Side-heads are headlines placed at the side of the page or column; they are most frequently set in italics with only the first word and proper names capitalized, sometimes in caps and small caps or bold face. A cut-in head is a head placed in a box cut into the side of the type-page, usually under the first two lines of the paragraph. A box-head is a head for a column in a ruled table. A running-head is a headline placed at the top of each page; it should be centered on the page regardless of page number and set two sizes smaller than text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow these typographic conventions for headline placement and style: center-heads/cut-in/side-heads have prescribed capitalization and placement; running-heads should be smaller than text and centered; choose between pyramid or hanging formats for multi-line center heads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraph types: plain vs hanging
rubrics_metrics.description: Two kinds of paragraphs are distinguished — plain and hanging. A plain (or regular) paragraph has the first line indented, and the others set flush. A hanging paragraph ('hanging indention') has the first line set flush, and the others indented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use plain paragraphs for standard prose; employ hanging indention where structure (lists, bibliographies, or certain stylistic effects) requires it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof definitions and workflow terms
rubrics_metrics.description: A galley-proof is an impression of the type contained in a galley; a page-proof is an impression made up into page-form; a plate-proof or foundry-proof is a proof taken of the type-page immediately before an electrotype cast is made; a joid proof is a galley-proof containing author's corrections; a revise is a new proof of type corrected from a marked proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand and use these distinct proof stages in the editorial/production workflow so corrections are applied at the correct stage and proofs are identified accurately (galley -> page -> plate -> revise, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Make-up and folio conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: The arranging into page-form of type-lines is called the make-up. A folio is a page-number: even numbers are placed on the verso; odd, on the recto. A drop-folio is a page-number placed at the bottom of a page. A half-title or bastard title is the abbreviated title of a book placed on a separate page preceding the full title-page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow standard make-up conventions for page numbering and preliminary title pages: place even folios on left (verso), odd on right (recto), and use half-title pages where customary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotype vs linotype spacing and machine implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Monotype composition uses an 18-unit quad unit system with fixed cast spaces and a swelling (justifying) space used on the keyboard to fill out a line; linotype uses the pica system with three fixed spaces (em quad, en quad, thin space) and a space band to spread a space between a 3-em and a trifle larger than an en quad. If a space smaller than a thin space is required it must be put in by hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of mechanical differences when preparing copy for monotype vs linotype composition: monotype has variable keyboard justification and unit-based fixed spaces; linotype relies on pica measures and the space band; small fine adjustments may require manual insertion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotype and linotype machine definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: The monotype is a composing-machine on which perforated paper patterns cast characters separately and arrange them in justified lines. The linotype is a composing-machine on which matrices arrange themselves in lines and cast a slug (a line of type).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When specifying production requirements, indicate which composing technology the shop will use, since methods of justification, spacing, and corrections differ between monotype and linotype workflows.
